list.title: apiPool.DEFAULT_WIDTH
list.description: Width for devices not on the low-memory list. Do not change without measuring on device (npm run measure) — see the doc above.

list.title: apiPool.LOW_MEMORY_WIDTH
list.description: Width for 512 MB devices (m.global.device.isLowMemoryDevice).

list.title: apiPool.currentWidth
list.description: The width this session's pool was created with (m.global.apiPoolWidth). Falls back to LOW_MEMORY_WIDTH when the field is absent — before setGlobalNodes() has run, or in a unit test — because asking for fewer slots than exist only queues requests, while asking for more would count slots that were never created. On a Task thread each call is a cross-thread read: call it once per run, not once per request.

list.title: apiPool.widthFor
list.description: The pool width for a device class. Called once, in setGlobalNodes().

list.title: apiResponse
list.description: Shape checks for parsed response bodies — the one place a caller learns whether a body holds what its endpoint promised, before it iterates or indexes it.

list.title: apiResponse.ERROR_ABANDONED
list.description: res.error value when the pool completed a queued read without sending it, because nobody was waiting for the answer any more (apiPool.settleIfCallerGone).

list.title: apiResponse.ERROR_UNEXPECTED_SHAPE
list.description: res.error value when a 200's body is not the shape its request expected.

list.title: apiResponse.EXPECT_LIST
list.description: req.expect value for an endpoint that answers with a bare array (ApiClient.listReq).

list.title: apiResponse.enforceShape
list.description:
Holds a pool response to the shape its request declared. ApiTask runs every response through this, so a caller of a list request never sees a body it cannot iterate.

For a request built with expect: "list", an ok response leaves with json set to the list (unwrapped by listFrom), or — when the body holds none — with ok = false, json = invalid and error = "unexpectedShape". statusCode stays the server's, so a log line still says what came back. Reporting it as not-ok is deliberate: every caller already treats not ok as "no answer", which is what an unreadable body is. Any other response is returned untouched.

list.title: apiResponse.expectsList
list.description: Whether a request declared that its endpoint answers with a bare array (ApiClient.listReq).

list.title: apiResponse.listFrom
list.description:
Returns the list a list endpoint answered with, or invalid when the body holds none.

BrightScript iterates an AA's KEYS, so a body that is an object instead of an array does not fail softly: for each item in json hands back key strings, and the first item.Field (or a json[0]) is a runtime error that kills the app.

Also accepts the { Items: [...] } query-result wrapper. Stock Jellyfin does not send it for bare-array endpoints, but a server has sent exactly that for /Items/Latest in the field, and its Items is the same list — so reading it shows the user their content where rejecting it would leave the row empty on every retry. The same property makes this the reader for a query-result endpoint too, when a caller wants its list and nothing else.

invalid means "no list", which callers must treat as NO ANSWER, not as an authoritative empty list — an empty array is returned as-is and is the only way to say "empty".

list.title: backoff
list.description: Exponential backoff for retrying something that failed: how long to wait before the next attempt, and whether a failure is still waiting that long. Pure — callers pass their own clock in, so the same failure state works on any thread and in a test.

list.title: backoff.afterFailure
list.description: The failure state after one more failure.

list.title: backoff.isWaiting
list.description: Whether failure is still waiting out its delay at nowMs. False for invalid: nothing failed.

list.title: backoff.nextDelayMs
list.description: The delay before the retry that follows a 0-based attempt: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, 16 s, then capped at 30 s.

list.title: cellLoad
list.description:
The cell-load ledger — how much work did a screen's CELLS do, and how much of it was waste?

Why this exists as a second ledger rather than more fields on screenLoad

screenReadiness.bs answers "when did this screen become usable and when did it stop changing" — a question with a beginning and an end, whose state lives on the SCREEN's m. This answers a different one: how many times were cells bound, and how much network did that cost. Two things force it apart:

  1. Cells are separate components, so they cannot reach the screen's m at all. screenReadiness's own header names this constraint and takes the same way out (a field the parent observes) for ExtrasRowList.contentReady.
  2. The interesting behaviour happens AFTER settle. A cell rebind storm during scrolling is invisible to a ledger that closes when the screen stops loading.

It deliberately keeps every other convention screenLoad established: namespaced free functions, the #if perfTiming gate INSIDE each sub so a shipped build compiles them to empty calls, one uniform emit shape so scripts/measurements.js needs ONE entry covering every screen present and future, and an instrumentUs that measures the instrument's own footprint rather than arguing about it.

Where the counters live, and why the content root

On the RowList / MarkupGrid content root — the same node initTextureManager already hangs loadedRowRange on, and the one every cell already holds a reference to (m.contentRoot). Three reasons it is the right home and not m.global:

  • Thread-local. All SceneGraph component code runs on the render thread, so a cell incrementing a content-root field never crosses a boundary. MEASURED on device rather than assumed, on HomeRows' root specifically because a Task also writes that node: 100 writes to a locally-created node took 351 us, 100 to the content root 379 us — ~3.8 us per write, a ratio of 1.08. A rendezvous would be orders of magnitude. ⚠️ An earlier version of this note said m.global is "main-thread-owned and WOULD cross". That is WRONG and was refuted by measurement 2026-08-23: m.global is RENDER-owned, so from a cell (render thread) it costs 2.0 us against a local node's 1.7 us — no crossing at all. It is 93 us from a Task thread. The content root is still the right home, on the two grounds below plus per-screen scoping; only the threading rationale was false. See docs/architecture/threading.md.
  • Race-free without any locking. The render thread is single-threaded, so read-modify-write across cells cannot interleave.
  • Free live readout. Node fields are readable over ODC, so a probe can watch the counters mid-scroll without waiting for an emit. There is no second mechanism.

The pop-in half — a race, not a count

appearances / popIns / popInsCold and the loadMs trio answer a different question from the counters above, and it is the one the texture buffer exists for. The buffer (±2 rows, and a 20-column window inside a long row) loads a cell's image BEFORE the cell is on screen so the user never watches a placeholder turn into a poster. Nothing observed whether it wins that race: every counter above measures work DONE, none measures work done IN TIME.

A pop-in is scored across two events, deliberately:

  1. appeared() — the cell is on screen. If its image is already there, nothing is pending and the race was won. If not, a pop-in is PENDING.
  2. loadSucceeded() — the image arrived. A pending pop-in resolves HERE, which is why the pending flag exists rather than a counter bump at step 1.

Resolving at step 2 is what keeps a broken image out of the number. An image that never arrives is not pop-in — the user sees a glyph, not a fade-in — and loadsFailed already counts it. Scoring at appearance time instead would make ExtrasRowList, where 117 of 140 loads fail against a real server, read as a total buffer failure when the buffer had nothing to do with it.

popInsCold splits the pop-ins by whether a request was even in flight when the cell appeared (isTextureUnloaded). Cold means the buffer never started the load — the cell came from outside the managed range, so the user outran the buffer's DEPTH. Not-cold means the buffer started in time and the network was slower, which more depth cannot fix. Two different remedies, one counter apart.

loadMs / loadMsCount / loadMsMax time each request from issue to ready. That is the image_load_time term in the buffer's own adequacy condition — buffer_depth × time_per_scroll_step >= image_load_time — and it is measured for EVERY load, including buffer preloads that never became visible, which are exactly the ones a depth decision needs. loadMsCount is carried rather than reusing loadsSucceeded because the two differ: a "ready" with no matching issue (Roku re-reporting a URI that was never re-requested) is a success with no interval to record. Dividing by the wrong count would be the inference-by-subtraction this ledger already refuses once.

Lifecycle — no per-screen call sites

Bound to the texture-manager lifecycle, which all five cell-bearing screens already drive: initTextureManager attaches the counters, hideTextureManager / destroyTextureManager emit them. Every content root already receives both, though often from its PARENT (Home hides HomeRows' root; ItemDetails hides and destroys ExtrasRowList's). So instrumenting a sixth screen costs nothing here — using the texture manager is the opt-in.

⚠️ Known limit, stated rather than hidden: a screen that REPLACES its content root starts a fresh set of counters, and the old root's counts die unemitted. BaseGridView does this at five call sites (refresh, filter change, …) and SearchRow at two. So a grid's line covers "since the last rebuild", not "since the screen opened". Fixable by emitting before the replace; deliberately not done in the first cut because it needs five call sites and the limit is visible in the numbers rather than silent.

list.title: cellLoad.FROM_CONTENT
list.description: Bind triggers. Which one fired is the whole point of splitting them: content is a cell being recycled onto new data (legitimate), size is a re-render caused by a layout change alone. MEASURED 2026-08-20 on ItemDetails + Home: 289 binds, ALL of them content and none size. So bindsFromSize is expected to be ZERO and is worth keeping precisely as a standing invariant — if it ever goes positive, a layout change has started re-issuing image requests, which is a regression with no other symptom.

list.title: cellLoad.UNLOAD_RANGE
list.description: Which mechanism evicted a resident texture. The texture manager has TWO, they answer to different dials, and the total cannot tell them apart: range - the cell fell outside the managed vertical range (loadedRowRange +/- 2 rows) and renderTracking decided. Driven by how far the user scrolled DOWN, and it fires on every screen including grids. window - the horizontal item window inside a VISIBLE row evicted the cell, which only happens on a RowList row holding more than TEXTURE_BUFFER_THRESHOLD items. This is the ONLY signal that horizontal windowing ran at all. The split exists because the total is dominated by range — Home reads ~57 unloads on a cell sweep with Limit: 16, where no row is long enough for window to be reachable — so "did raising the per-row limit engage windowing?" is unanswerable from unloads. Both are emitted rather than one plus the total, so neither is derived by subtraction.

list.title: cellLoad.WIPE_BIND
list.description: Which path wiped a failure glyph back to the loading state. Both are visible flicker, but they are not equally bad and the split is what tells them apart: a bind wipe lands on a cell whose content is changing anyway, while a reload wipe hits a cell that is SITTING STILL showing a stable glyph — which is what reads to a user as blinking for no reason.

list.title: cellLoad.appeared
list.description:
The cell is on screen. One half of the pop-in race; loadSucceeded is the other.

hasTexture is the caller's read of its own poster's loadStatus, and it is deliberately NOT trusted alone. A request issued and not yet resolved means the texture currently on screen belongs to the cell's PREVIOUS item while loadStatus still reads "ready" from it — established behaviour, not supposition: JRRowItem.renderItem's same-URI shortcut exists precisely because Roku leaves loadStatus alone until a new request resolves. Trusting it alone would under-count exactly the recycled-cell case pop-in is about.

Counted at most ONCE per EPISODE, an episode being bind -> visible -> gone. Ungated otherwise, deliberately: an appearance is idempotent within an episode, so calling this from both renderItem and onRenderTrackingChanged cannot double-count, and first paint legitimately happens before activateTextureManager runs. The episode is closed only by bind and departed, and it is departed — not this — that carries the state gate keeping a spurious compositor flip from re-arming it.

list.title: cellLoad.attach
list.description:
Attach counters to a content root. Called by initTextureManager, so every screen that uses the texture manager is instrumented without its own call site.

BrighterScript does not schema-check the dynamic fields below against ContentNode's declared interface. screenLoad.begin and for the same reason: the screen an operator navigated to is established by the nav, not by the app.

list.title: cellLoad.bind
list.description: One cell bind. isRedundant is the cell's own answer to "did I just bind this exact item at this exact size again?" — kept on the CELL because its previous bind is free to remember there and would cost a node round trip to store here.

list.title: cellLoad.bump
list.description: Increment one counter. Extracted so the single-counter call sites above do not each repeat the guard, and so the instrument's own cost is accumulated in one place rather than in each of them, where it could drift. A counter that bumps a TOTAL and a SPLIT together (bind, unload) does it inline instead — one event should clock the probe once, not twice. Deliberately no call-site COUNT here: the number this comment used to carry said nine against an actual four, which is what a hand-maintained enumeration does. grep -n 'bump(contentRoot' source/utils/cellLoad.bs answers it.

list.title: cellLoad.cellState
list.description:
Per-CELL instrument state, cached on the caller's m exactly as probe() is.

One AA rather than four bare m fields so every flag is a real boolean from its first read. An unset m.someFlag is Invalid, and if Invalid is a &h18 type mismatch rather than a falsy check — the fault class behind the EnableFallbackFont crash. Initialising the whole set together makes that unreachable by construction instead of by every call site remembering a guard.

list.title: cellLoad.countItems
list.description:
Total ITEMS under a content root, which is the denominator of the rebind rate and is NOT getChildCount(). The two content shapes disagree about what a child is: a MarkupGrid root is flat, so its children ARE the items, while a RowList root is two level and its children are ROWS. Using the child count for both would have divided Home's binds by its ~10 rows instead of its ~68 items and published a "rebind rate" an order of magnitude wrong — in a field that looks equally plausible either way.

Detected by shape rather than by a flag the caller has to pass correctly: a root whose first child has children of its own is hierarchical. Walked once per emit, never per bind.

list.title: cellLoad.departed
list.description:
The cell LEFT the screen. Ends the appearance episode, so a later return counts as a NEW appearance rather than being swallowed by the once-per-bind gate.

🚨 This is what makes the re-entry race measurable at all, and its absence silently hollowed out the metric. A RowList / MarkupGrid does NOT rebind a cell that scrolls off and back onto the SAME item — onItemContentChanged never fires — so with the gate re-arming only on bind, every scroll-back was skipped. Measured on cellSweepGrid: binds 28 against 28 items, i.e. nothing was rebound all sweep, while 7 reloads happened; all 7 re-entry races went unevaluated and the ledger still published a confident-looking popInsReload 1. The one thing the buffer exists to win was the one thing not being counted.

A pending pop-in is dropped here rather than carried: a cell that appeared without its image and then went away was never watched fading in, so a late arrival is not a pop-in.

⚠️ CALLER'S OBLIGATION: only call this while the texture manager is "active". A renderTracking of "none" during init is a layout recalculation and during hidden is visible=false propagating — neither is a departure, and closing the episode on one makes the screen's return score a fresh appearance nobody saw. Both cell components gate the call for this; evaluateTextureState refuses the same two states already. The INVARIANT is what to remember — on a resume with no scrolling, every appearance has to be paid for by a bind. Measured before the gate against the demo server: 18 appearances against 10 binds, all non-pop-ins, inflating the denominator that popIns / appearances divides by. The counts are that fixture's; the bound is the app's, and it is gated in tests/rta/specs/cell-load.spec.js.

⚠️ Deliberately NOT probed into instrumentUs, unlike every other entry point here. Measured on cellSweepGrid against a real server (.177, n=5, same fixture and identical workload in both arms): adding the probe took instrumentUs 7371 -> 8411 µs, +1040 µs / +14.1%. Absolute µs are that fixture's; the RATIO is the point — for a body that is two AA assignments and no node write. That delta IS the probe — an roTimespan pair plus a render-thread read-modify-write on cellLoadInstrumentUs — so probing here would make the instrument meaningfully more expensive to report a figure that is almost entirely the measurement apparatus. instrumentUs is therefore a LOWER BOUND by this much.

list.title: cellLoad.emit
list.description: Emit the session's counters and reset them. Called by hideTextureManager (the user navigated away — a complete viewing session) and destroyTextureManager (teardown). Emitting on BOTH is why cellLoadEmitted exists: a screen that is hidden and then destroyed must publish one line, not two, and a second line of zeroes would read as a real session in which nothing happened.

list.title: cellLoad.glyphWipe
list.description: A failure glyph was reset to the loading state. See WIPE_* for why the source matters.

list.title: cellLoad.loadErrored
list.description:
An image request came back failed. loadsFailed far exceeding the number of distinct broken images is the signature of a retry with no memory of the last failure.

⚠️ NAMED loadErrored RATHER THAN loadFailed, and it must stay that way. Rooibos's transpiler mistakes a namespaced call whose method name it reads as an assertion for a call ON THE TEST SUITE, and rewrites its own bookkeeping against the NAMESPACE instead of m — cellLoad.currentAssertLineNumber = 148, cellLoad_done(). That is a compile-time rewrite producing code that crashes with "Use of uninitialized variable" at runtime, and only in the spec, so the app is fine while the suite reports a crash it cannot explain. The emitted LOG FIELD is still loadsFailed — the wire format is what scripts/measurements.js reads and it is unaffected by this rename.

list.title: cellLoad.loadStarted
list.description: An image request was issued (the poster URI was assigned a real URL). Also starts this cell's load clock — see the pop-in section of the header for why the interval matters more than the count.

list.title: cellLoad.loadSucceeded
list.description: An image request came back ready. Its job is not the count itself but the RESIDUAL: loadsStarted - (loadsFailed + loadsSucceeded) is the number of requests still in flight when the session was emitted, and at a quiescent boundary it should be zero. Without it, an outstanding request is indistinguishable from a success — every "successful loads" figure was an inference subtracting one counter from another, with nothing able to check it. See waitCellsQuiet in tests/rta/lib/steps.js, which watches this counter for the same reason it watches loadsFailed.

list.title: cellLoad.loadTimer
list.description: The cell's LOAD clock, distinct from probe() because it spans a network round trip rather than a single call — one roTimespan cannot carry two marks.

list.title: cellLoad.probe
list.description:
The instrument's own stopwatch, created ONCE per cell and reused.

m here is the CALLING component's — these are namespaced free functions, the same mechanism screenReadiness.bs relies on — so this caches on the cell, which is exactly the right lifetime: one per pooled cell rather than one per event.

Measured before this existed, on a Home load: 15458 us across ~706 counter calls, or ~22 us each, against ~3.8 us for the field write the call is actually making. So the STOPWATCH was five times the cost of the thing it was timing. screenReadiness.bs warns about precisely this ("a fresh roTimespan per ledger call would make the measurement of the overhead a significant part of the overhead") and this repeated it anyway; instrumentUs is what caught it, which is the argument for carrying that field at all.

list.title: cellLoad.reset
list.description: Zero the counters for the next session. cellLoadEmitted is cleared LAST so a hidden screen that is shown again starts a fresh, emittable session.

list.title: cellLoad.unload
list.description: A resident texture was released. reason says which mechanism did it — see UNLOAD_* for why the split is the whole point of this counter.

list.title: collectionsView
list.description:
The per-library Collections view — a Jellyfin 12.0 server capability.

GET /Items?parentId=<library>&IncludeItemTypes=BoxSet is a request every supported server answers with HTTP 200, and that is exactly the problem: what changed in 12.0 is whether the server HONOURS the scope. Measured on the local 10.11.11 / 12.0.0 / 12.1.0 servers, 2026-09-23, against a fixture holding one collection of films from HDR Movies and one from Movies:

On 12.x the scope is correct. HDR Movies returns its own collection, Movies returns its own, and the Shows TV library returns 0. On 10.11 with Recursive=true the scope is IGNORED: every one of those three libraries returns BOTH collections, the TV library included. On 10.11 with Recursive=false it is worse still — IncludeItemTypes is ignored too, and the response is the user's ten root library folders (CollectionFolder / ManualPlaylistsFolder items) rather than collections at all.

So there is no degraded-but-honest pre-12.0 behavior to fall back on: the view would show another library's collections, or a list of libraries. The two failure directions also mean no response shape distinguishes a server that scoped from one that did not — a 10.11 answer is a well-formed 200 with plausible items — which is why the gate is on the SERVER VERSION rather than on anything observable in the reply.

Playlists are deliberately not offered alongside. Playlist + parentId on 10.11 fails the opposite way (it returns 0 for the library whose films the playlist holds), but the reason to leave it out is not the version: a playlist is user-made and cross-cutting, and a top-level Playlists library already browses it.

list.title: collectionsView.MIN_SERVER
list.description: The first server line that scopes parentId for BoxSet queries. Below it the same request succeeds and answers wrongly, so this is a gate, not an optimization.

list.title: collectionsView.VIEW_NAME
list.description: The view's Name in a presenter's views list, in the saved landing display setting, and in the viewMode a presenter is configured with. Shared so the presenters, the query branch and the title branch cannot drift apart on spelling.

list.title: collectionsView.offeredFor
list.description:
offeredFor: Whether a grid's View menu lists Collections — on the library itself, and only on a server that scopes the query.

Not inside a studio, network or genre folder, although 12.x answers those queries correctly. A collection's studios and genres are the union of its films', so a folder-scoped list holds every collection with even ONE film matching — a mixed collection turns up under a genre most of it is not. The view means "this library's collections" and is offered only where it can mean exactly that.

list.title: collectionsView.supported
list.description:
supported: Whether this server scopes a per-library BoxSet query.

unknown server is assumed not to scope, so the view is not offered rather than offered and quietly wrong)

list.title: episodeQueue
list.description:
One entry per episode in a queue the app builds from a list of episodes — the next episodes behind the one playing, Play All, quick play and shuffle of a series, season, person or folder.

Before 12.0 the server lists every file of an episode as its own episode (same series, season and episode number, one MediaSource each — the same on 10.7 through 10.11), so a plain queue plays both copies back to back. Copies are grouped and one is kept, chosen like a version: the viewer's explicit pick when a copy matches it, else the best for the device (versionPick). A 12.0 server merges them into one item with alternate versions, so its lists have no copies and nothing here costs a request.

Playlists and collections are left alone: the viewer put those entries there.

Everything but collapseCopies() / collapseQueue() is pure, so the rules are unit-tested without a network seam.

list.title: episodeQueue.chooseCopy
list.description:
chooseCopy: The one copy of an episode to queue, by the same rule as a version.

A copy's own source is its FIRST MediaSource: before 12.0 each copy is a separate item with its file as its only source. When any copy's sources could not be read, the server's first copy is kept — a choice made on partial data would be a guess.

list.title: episodeQueue.collapseCopies
list.description:
collapseCopies: The items with one copy per episode, in play order.

The imperative shell around the rules above; runs on a Task thread. MediaSources are fetched only when copies exist — mediaSources.byIds() chunks them — so a 12.0 list (never any copies) costs nothing.

list.title: episodeQueue.collapseQueue
list.description:
collapseQueue: A whole queue with one copy per episode.

exact copy stays first (its position is its own), and its episode's other copies are dropped

list.title: episodeQueue.copyIds
list.description: copyIds: The ids of every item that has another copy in its group — the only items whose MediaSources are needed to choose between them.

list.title: episodeQueue.episodeKey
list.description:
episodeKey: "/SE" for a single numbered episode, "" otherwise.

"" means "never group": anything that is not an episode (a movie, a recording, a track — which has disc and track numbers), an episode without a series or numbers, and a multi-episode file (IndexNumberEnd past IndexNumber), which covers more than the episode its first number names. The series is part of the key so a list mixing shows never merges S1E1 of one with S1E1 of another.

list.title: episodeQueue.groupByEpisode
list.description:
groupByEpisode: The items as groups of copies of one episode, in the order each episode first appears. An item that cannot be keyed is a group of its own.

other copies would otherwise play it a second time

list.title: episodeQueue.inProgressCopy
list.description:
inProgressCopy: The copy the viewer is partway through, or invalid. With more than one, the one played most recently (LastPlayedDate is ISO 8601, so it compares as text).

A resume must come from this copy: its position belongs to its own file, and copies of one episode can differ in runtime.

list.title: episodeQueue.isGroupPlayed
list.description: isGroupPlayed: Whether the viewer has watched this episode — on ANY copy. Before 12.0 each copy keeps its own watched state, so an unwatched copy of a watched episode is not a reason to play it again.

list.title: extrasLayout.ACTION_SAFE_BOTTOM_Y
list.description: Roku 5% action-safe bottom edge (1080 - 54). Extras rows must not render below this.

list.title: extrasLayout.PANEL_CLOSED_Y
list.description: Y position of extrasGrp when the panel is off-screen (closed). Matches the extrasGrp initial translation and VertSlider start keyValue in ExtrasSlider.xml.

list.title: extrasLayout.PANEL_OPEN_Y
list.description: Y position of extrasGrp when the panel is fully open (screen space). Matches the VertSlider end keyValue and extrasGrp open translation in ExtrasSlider.xml.

list.title: extrasRows
list.description:
Decision layer for ItemDetails' extras rows — which rows an item type shows, in what order and slot shape, how a delivered row is ordered and filtered, when a run may be committed to the RowList and which rows it may skip, and the layout arrays for the rows on screen.

It lives in source/ rather than in ExtrasRowList.bs because a component codebehind's functions are scoped to that component: a Rooibos suite cannot call them without a callFunc seam on the XML. Same move as source/home/latestRows.bs.

Everything here is pure: no nodes are created, no fields written, no translation looked up. A plan row names its title by translation key so the consumer resolves it on the render thread, and the item argument may be a node or an AA.

list.title: extrasRows.ITEM_COLLECTIONS_MIN_SERVER
list.description: The first Jellyfin release that can list the collections an item is in (GET /Items/{itemId}/Collections). Older servers answer 404.

list.title: extrasRows.appendCastAndDiscovery
list.description: Cast, then the discovery tail — how every video-library type ends except those on the Movie plan, which put Special Features between the two.

list.title: extrasRows.appendDiscovery
list.description: Collections, then More Like This — the rows that lead away from the item.

list.title: extrasRows.collectionsRow
list.description: The collections the item is in. Keyed on the item ITSELF, even for an episode, unlike More Like This: the server lists only the collections an item was added to directly, so asking about an episode's series would show collections the episode is not in. PORTRAIT whatever the viewed item's shape — the tiles are collections, not items like this one.

list.title: extrasRows.commitActions
list.description:
What committing a resolved run does to each plan row. The caller applies it to the RowList; nothing here touches a node.

did not load that row actions - one per plan row: "write" build the row from its result, or rewrite the one on screen "leave" the row on screen stays exactly as it is "remove" the row on screen goes "none" there is no row, before or after isStructureChanged - true when a row appears, disappears or changes slot shape, which is the only time the RowList layout needs writing playlistContentKind - the kind of the playlist row as committed ("unknown" when it is not on screen), or invalid when the plan has no playlist row

list.title: extrasRows.currentFirst
list.description: The current item, then the items after it, then the items before it — e.g. viewing episode 3 of 5 gives [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]. Server order is kept when the item is absent.

list.title: extrasRows.digestOf
list.description:
A digest identifying a row's source content.

Taken over the exact text the row is built from (the HTTP response body, on the Task thread that already holds it) rather than over the item nodes: comparing every field of every node on the render thread measured 252-306 ms per Refresh on a Stick 4K for a three-row movie.

list.title: extrasRows.finishRow
list.description:
Orders, filters and (for playlists) re-shapes and classifies one delivered row.

a playlist row, and "" for every other row

list.title: extrasRows.isRowUnchanged
list.description:
Is a delivered row identical to the one on screen? Such a row is not written at all: RowList redraws its row counter on any write to an on-screen row, even one that changes nothing.

Identity is the title plus a digest of the row's SOURCE content — the server's response body, or the item data a local row is built from — taken where that content is at hand (see digestOf). Anything the server changes about the row, including a field on an item whose id did not change (its played state, an image tag), changes the digest; so an unchanged digest means the rebuilt row would be identical, and a tile can never be left showing stale data.

An empty digest means the content could not be identified, and is never treated as unchanged: the row is rewritten, which is correct if it costs a counter redraw.

list.title: extrasRows.isRunResolved
list.description: Has every slot of a run resolved? A run is committed to the RowList only then, in one pass.

list.title: extrasRows.itemsFromResponse
list.description:
The raw items one extras response lets its row show, or invalid when the row must be treated as "failed".

Only an ok response whose body holds a list is authoritative. No answer, a not-ok response, and an ok body with no list in it all return invalid: none says what the item HAS, and an "ok" with an empty list REMOVES the row (rowDisposition). The list is read through apiResponse.listFrom, so a bare-array endpoint (Special Features) and a query result ({ Items }, every other row) take the same path.

list.title: extrasRows.plan
list.description:
The ordered rows for an item type.

Each row is an AA: kind - what to fetch; the orchestrator maps it to a request ("chapters" and "cast" are built from the item itself, with no request) shape - "PORTRAIT" | "WIDE" | "SQUARE"; finishRow may revise it (playlists) titleKey - translation key; titleArgs holds its placeholders when it has any itemId - the id the request is keyed on seasonId - season rows only currentId - rows that put the viewed item first excludeId - rows that drop the viewed item

A row whose request cannot be formed for this item (an episode with no season, a track with no album) is left out of the plan rather than planned and resolved empty.

Rows about the item itself come first; the rows that lead AWAY from it — Collections, then More Like This — come last on every type that has them (appendDiscovery).

Every type plans a Collections row except Person. The server accepts any item into a collection, so none is ruled out by type; the row simply stays off screen when the answer is empty. Person's rows are the person's own media instead: ExtrasRowList.finishRunIfResolved reads "any row on screen" as personHasMedia, which shows the Shuffle button, so a Collections row there would offer to shuffle a person with nothing to play.

planned (supportsItemCollections)

list.title: extrasRows.playlistContentKind
list.description:
What a playlist holds, for ItemDetails' Watched button and "Tracks"/"Items" label.

"unknown" covers both an empty playlist and one that failed to load — ItemDetails treats it as the safe default (no Watched button, "Items" label).

list.title: extrasRows.rowDisposition
list.description:
What a resolved row does to the list.

A failed request says nothing about what the item HAS, so it never removes a row — the same rule latestRows.drainReady applies to Home. Only an answered, empty row removes one.

list.title: extrasRows.rowSizes
list.description: RowList layout for the rows on screen: one slot and one row height per row, in order.

list.title: extrasRows.supportsItemCollections
list.description:
Whether the server can list the collections an item is in (GET /Items/{itemId}/Collections).

Older servers answer 404, so the Collections row is left out of the plan there rather than requested and failed. Registered as a version guard in docs/dev/jellyfin-endpoint-availability.yml, whose lint fails if this function disappears.

list.title: focusableOverview.FOCUS_OUTSET
list.description: How far the focus border is drawn OUTSIDE the text on each side, when the overview has no background (and so no padding of its own to draw it in). A screen that bounds the overview's text subtracts this to keep the focused border inside the same bound.

list.title: gridQuery
list.description:
The library grid's LoadItemsTask2 query — what BaseGridView asks for, kept apart from the Task node that runs it.

BaseGridView runs every load and every page on a NEW node (see replaceTask), so the node cannot be the memory of the query: the next page must ask for exactly what the first page asked for, and that has to survive the node being replaced. The query is a plain AA held on the component instead, and paging.forPage gives each page its copy.

It lives in source/ rather than in BaseGridView.bs because a component codebehind's functions are scoped to that component and a Rooibos suite cannot call them without a callFunc seam on the XML. Same move as source/home/latestRows.bs.

list.title: gridQuery.build
list.description: The query for a fresh load: the defaults, then whatever the presenter sets for its view. Presenters receive a plain AA and assign fields on it exactly as they would on a LoadItemsTask2 node. Built from scratch every time, so nothing a presenter set for one view carries into the next.

list.title: gridQuery.checkedStateFor
list.description:
checkedStateFor: which of a category's options a saved query has selected.

The inverse of queryValueFor(), and the reason the pair has to be tested together: this is what re-ticks the boxes when the panel reopens, matching on the VALUE because that is what was saved — the registry holds the query the filter applied, not the labels it was picked by.

list.title: gridQuery.isFilterOptionPair
list.description:
Whether an option carries a separate label and value, rather than being its own.

A plain and would not do here: BrightScript does not short-circuit it, so a validity guard and a member access cannot share one condition.

list.title: gridQuery.offersView
list.description:
offersView: whether viewName is one of the views the presenter is listing.

Case-insensitive, matching how BaseGridView.SetUpOptions already compares a view name to the saved one — a presenter's Name and the saved string must agree under the same rule in both places or a view could restore here and fail to tick there.

list.title: gridQuery.optionTitle
list.description: optionTitle: what the user sees for one selectable option.

list.title: gridQuery.optionValue
list.description: optionValue: what the request carries for one selectable option.

list.title: gridQuery.optionValues
list.description: optionValues: every option's query value, in the order the panel lists them.

list.title: gridQuery.queryValueFor
list.description:
queryValueFor: the saved query for one category — its checked options' values, joined.

Takes VALUES rather than options because the caller (ItemGridOptions) reads them off the CheckList's own nodes, not off the presenter's option list; optionValues() is the bridge for callers that hold the list instead.

list.title: gridQuery.resolveView
list.description:
resolveView: which view a load should actually use.

savedView is Invalid when the library has never had one chosen, which is the common case and is answered with the default exactly as before. A saved name is honored unless the presenter has stopped offering it.

THE EMPTY DEFAULT IS NOT A MISSING VIEW. getDefaultView() returns "" for the Live TV, Photos and Generic presenters, whose grids run with no named view at all — and "" is in no presenter's list, so a rule of "reset anything not offered" would reset those on every load. Only a non-empty saved name is checked.

The caller does NOT write the fallback back to the registry: the saved choice is still what the user picked, and it becomes valid again the moment the library is opened against a server that supports it.

list.title: guidePrograms
list.description:
Which program blocks the TV guide (Schedule) should hold, fetch next, and drop.

The guide loads every channel row but programs only near the viewport: every channel's programs at once do not fit a large lineup on a 512 MB device. Programs are fetched in BLOCKS of BLOCK_SIZE consecutive channel rows — one request per block — and at most CAP blocks hold programs at once. They hold them only for a TIME WINDOW around the grid's left edge (timeWindow), not from the guide's start: a block holding every program up to a horizon that only grows ran a 512 MB device out of memory once the user looked a few days ahead. So program memory is bounded by CAP blocks x the window, whatever the lineup size and the day.

Pure decisions only: the component does the fetching and the node writes. A block's state is in held (an AA keyed by the block index as a string), absent when it holds nothing, else { from, until, stale }: it holds every program airing in [from, until] (seconds since the epoch) — those ending at or after from and starting at or before until, as one /LiveTv/Programs query with MinEndDate and MaxStartDate returns them. stale marks programs that must be replaced (a series was recorded). A block whose last fetch failed also has an entry in failures (same keys): its backoff state (source/utils/backoff.bs), so it is not fetched again until its retryAt. Times in failures are on the component's own millisecond clock, not the epoch.

list.title: guidePrograms.BLOCK_SIZE
list.description: Channels per program request. 25 channels x 24 h is ~460 programs on the fixture server.

list.title: guidePrograms.BUFFER_ROWS
list.description: Rows kept near either side of the visible rows: one whole block, so the next block is already loading by the time the user reaches it.

list.title: guidePrograms.CAP
list.description: Blocks that may hold programs at once. At most four are ever wanted (the visible rows plus BUFFER_ROWS either side can touch four blocks), so this keeps a couple of recently visited blocks for scrolling back without refetching.

list.title: guidePrograms.NEED_BEFORE
list.description: A block is fetched again only once it covers less than NEED_BEFORE / NEED_AFTER around the left edge, so pressing Left or Right does not start a fetch each time.

list.title: guidePrograms.TRIM_SLACK
list.description: Programs more than this outside the window are trimmed.

list.title: guidePrograms.WINDOW_BEFORE
list.description: The time window blocks load programs for: WINDOW_BEFORE before the left edge to WINDOW_AFTER after it (seconds).

list.title: guidePrograms.blockOf
list.description: The block a row belongs to.

list.title: guidePrograms.blockRows
list.description: The rows of block present in the grid, as [first, last] inclusive.

list.title: guidePrograms.evictions
list.description: Blocks to drop so at most cap hold programs: never a wanted one, farthest from the focused block first. The guide passes CAP.

list.title: guidePrograms.fetchFor
list.description: The fetch that brings a block holding state up to the window: only the side it is missing when what it holds overlaps the window, else the whole window in place of what it holds.

list.title: guidePrograms.isBlockReady
list.description: Whether every row of block has arrived.

list.title: guidePrograms.isCurrent
list.description: Whether key's block covers enough of the window to need no fetch. A stale block never does.

list.title: guidePrograms.isWanted
list.description: Whether block is one of wanted.

list.title: guidePrograms.nextFetch
list.description: The next fetch to make, or invalid when every wanted block covers the window or is waiting to retry. Fetches are made one at a time; call again after each lands.

list.title: guidePrograms.nextRetryAt
list.description: When the earliest wanted block waiting to retry may be fetched, or invalid when none is waiting — the time to come back if nextFetch has nothing to do now.

list.title: guidePrograms.pruneFailures
list.description: failures with only the wanted blocks' entries, so a block the focus comes back to later starts again from the first, shortest delay.

list.title: guidePrograms.spanState
list.description: What rows in [firstRow, lastRow] without programs should say — TimeGrid has one text for every such row. FAILED wins over LOADING: a block waiting up to 30 s to retry must not read as loading, while a block still loading next to it reads as unavailable only until it lands.

list.title: guidePrograms.timeWindow
list.description:
The time window blocks should hold programs for, from the grid's left edge.

need no fetch; keepFrom / keepUntil, outside which what a block holds is trimmed

list.title: guidePrograms.trims
list.description:
What to cut back so blocks hold programs only near the window, farthest from the focus first: a block no longer wanted that holds anything outside [keepFrom, keepUntil] is dropped whole (coming back to it loads its own window anyway), as is a wanted one that no longer overlaps the window at all; any other wanted one is cut back to the window on the side that ran past it. The drops come before the cuts.

until to keep

list.title: guidePrograms.wantedBlocks
list.description: Blocks to hold programs for, nearest the focused row first: the focused block, then alternately below and above it. Only blocks whose rows have all arrived are listed — a block fetched while its channels are still paging in would miss the late ones.

list.title: homeScreenLoad
list.description:
Decision layer for Home's screen-load milestones — when has Home PAINTED?

Home's rows fill from several independent tasks, so no single handler is "the" paint. The ledger (source/utils/screenReadiness.bs) declares one fill per row, keyed by sectionId, and this decides when the rows the user is LOOKING AT have all landed:

paint - every row in the visible span has resolved (data, empty, or failed) settled - every row has resolved; the ledger derives that on its own

"Visible" is the span textureManager already maintains in loadedRowRange — the same signal cells use to decide which textures to load, and the one lazy row hydration would key on. It is [focusedRow, focusedRow + numRows - 1], which is the app's definition of the viewport rather than a measurement of pixels on screen.

Lives in source/ rather than in HomeRows.bs for the same reason as latestRows.bs: a Rooibos suite cannot call a component's functions without a callFunc seam on the XML.

list.title: homeScreenLoad.visibleRowsResolved
list.description:
Have all rows in the visible span resolved?

Rows only get SHORTER between the range being computed and this being asked — nothing recomputes loadedRowRange when a row is removed, only on focus changes — so the end of the span is clamped to the rows that exist now. Rows that shift up into the span after a removal are therefore counted, which is what the user sees.

An unset range on a non-empty row list answers false rather than true: painting on a range nobody computed would publish a paint time that describes no viewport. The run then never settles, which the measurement tooling reports as unmeasurable — the loud failure.

list.title: languageFilters
list.description:
Audio- and subtitle-language browse filters, a Jellyfin 12.0 server capability.

audioLanguages / subtitleLanguages are the only GET /Items parameters added between the 10.11.8 and 12.0 spec fingerprints (jellyfin#9787). Measured on the local 10.11.11 / 12.0.0 / 12.1.0 servers, 2026-09-22:

On 12.x they filter. audioLanguages=zzz returns 0 of 17 films; =eng returns all 17. On 10.11 they are SILENTLY IGNORED — audioLanguages=zzz returns all 17, in either casing. That is why the filters are version-gated rather than offered everywhere and allowed to no-op: a 10.11 user picking "Japanese audio" would get their whole library back, which reads as a broken filter. Within one parameter the values are OR'd (hin,pol returns exactly the union, 2 films); across the two parameters they are AND'd (Spanish audio 3, Japanese subtitles 9, both together 2). The panel can only have one filter category active at a time, so only the OR half is reachable today — see itemgridoptions-single-active-filter in tech-debt.md. Comma is the delimiter ON THE WIRE, and a pipe returns 0 there. It is NOT what the categories declare: an option's value is itself several comma-joined codes, so the panel separates options with PANEL_DELIMITER and toWire() flattens the two apart when the request is built. See PANEL_DELIMITER for why. Values are case-sensitive 3-letter ISO 639-2 codes. ENG and en both return 0. So the option list must send the server's own Value verbatim, which is why nothing here upper- or lower-cases a code.

THE ALIAS TRAP, and why this module exists at all. The server does NOT canonicalize ISO 639-2/T against /B: it matches the literal tag on the file. On the same library, subtitleLanguages=fra returns 1 film and fre returns 10, and /Items/Filters2 duly advertises BOTH as separate options — "French (fra)" and "French (fre)". Offering those two entries as the server sends them would be a filter where picking "French" gives one of two partial answers and which one is arbitrary. Grouping them and sending fra,fre returns all 11, which is what the user meant.

The grouping needs no new table: languageBaseCode() already folds the alias pairs (it is the same fold the audio/subtitle track pickers use), and resolveLanguageName() already localizes a code through the app's own language keys. Checked 2026-09-22 against the 52 codes the local fixture reports — every one resolves, and the 8 alias pairs present (fra/fre, deu/ger, ces/cze, nld/dut, zho/chi, eus/baq, ell/gre, ron/rum) merge cleanly.

Using the app's names rather than the server's Name is also what makes the list readable: the server's strings are English-only library-science labels ("Spanish; Castilian (spa)", "Greek, Modern (1453-) (ell)"), and the app already holds localized names for the same codes.

list.title: languageFilters.AUDIO_KEY
list.description: The key each category is stored and sent under. Shared by the presenter that declares the category, the Filters2 merge that fills it, and toWire(), so the three cannot drift apart on spelling.

list.title: languageFilters.CODE_DELIMITER
list.description: Separates the codes WITHIN one language's value, and is what the server requires between values. Comma is not a preference: a pipe-separated list returns 0 results.

list.title: languageFilters.MIN_SERVER
list.description: The first server line that honours the parameters at all. Below this they are accepted and ignored, so the gate is on the SERVER VERSION and not on whether the request succeeds.

list.title: languageFilters.PANEL_DELIMITER
list.description:
Separates the selected options from EACH OTHER, in the panel and in the registry.

It cannot also be CODE_DELIMITER, and that is the whole reason this constant exists. One language's value is already several codes joined by a comma ("fra,fre"), so a comma between options makes the saved query ambiguous: the restore pass splits "fra,fre" into "fra" and "fre", matches neither against the option, and leaves the box unticked while the filter is still applied — and one confirming keypress on that panel then clears the filter outright. Measured on a Roku Stick 2026-09-22: the round-trip test fails on exactly the 8 alias-merged languages and passes on the rest, which is what makes the bug look like flakiness rather than breakage.

"|" is what Genres and OfficialRatings already use for the same reason — their values are free text that can contain a comma — so this follows the panel's existing rule rather than inventing one: AN OPTION'S VALUE NEVER CONTAINS ITS CATEGORY'S DELIMITER. toWire() flattens the two apart on the way to the request.

list.title: languageFilters.isLanguageKey
list.description:
isLanguageKey: whether a filterOptions key is one of the two language categories.

Case-insensitive because the key round-trips through the registry as JSON and through a SceneGraph assocarray field, neither of which promises to preserve the spelling a presenter declared.

list.title: languageFilters.optionsFrom
list.description:
optionsFrom: Turn one /Items/Filters2 language list into filter options, merging the ISO 639-2/T and /B spellings of a language into a single entry.

Filters2 response: an array of { Name, Value }. Anything else (invalid, empty, not an array) is answered with an empty array, which the caller reads as "do not offer this category". value is every code that resolved to the same language, comma-joined

list.title: languageFilters.supported
list.description:
supported: Whether this server honours the language filter parameters.

an unknown server is assumed not to filter, so the categories are hidden rather than offered and silently ignored)

list.title: languageFilters.toWire
list.description:
toWire: the request form of a saved filterOptions AA.

The panel and the registry separate selected options with PANEL_DELIMITER; the server wants one flat comma list. Flattening that one level is the entire conversion — "fra,fre|deu,ger" becomes "fra,fre,deu,ger" — and it is what lets the saved form stay unambiguous while the sent form stays what the server accepts.

Only the two language keys are touched. Every other category already stores exactly what it sends, so its value is copied through untouched.

Called from gridQuery.build(), which is the single place a saved filterOptions becomes a request (LoadItemsTask2 appends whatever keys it is handed). Keeping the conversion there is what keeps the panel, the registry and the wire in agreement.

list.title: latestRows
list.description:
Decision layer for Home's latest-media rows — which of the orchestrator's delivered results the UI may act on, and where the drain cursor lands.

It lives in source/ rather than in HomeRows.bs because a component codebehind's functions are scoped to that component: a Rooibos suite (which runs in the source scope) cannot call them without a callFunc seam on the XML. Extracting the judgment instead keeps the seam off the component and the rules under test. Same move as source/remotecontrol/remoteCommand.bs.

list.title: latestRows.drainReady
list.description:
Walks LoadLatestRowsTask's result children from startIndex and returns the ones the UI should populate, plus the new cursor. One wake can cover several results — wake events coalesce, appended children don't — so the caller always drains to the end.

A "failed" child is SKIPPED, not returned. A timeout, a transport failure or an HTTP error says nothing about what the library holds, and populateRowFromData removes a row when handed an empty list — so acting on a failure would delete good content on a flaky refresh. The cursor still advances past it; the row self-heals on the next Home.refresh(), which fires on every onScreenShown.

DELIBERATELY does not hand failures back for the caller to clear the row. A latest row that has not been populated yet is not empty — insertLatestMediaSkeletons gives it one type: "Loading" placeholder child so the RowList renders it at the right slot size — so a failed row keeps that skeleton, and the next successful refresh fills it via populateRowFromData's "update children in place" branch: items appended, placeholder dropped, no insert. Removing the row instead would send that refresh down the else-branch, which CreateObject+insertChild's a fresh row — the row visibly pops in and shifts every row below it. Measured on device (8 libraries, HTTP 500 forced on five): the skipped rows sat at their single placeholder child and nothing shifted. Keep it that way.

Also resets silenceClock whenever the drain moves past at least one child — a failed child included, since it is still the run reporting in. runIsStalled reads that clock, and the reset lives here rather than at the call site because this is the one call every delivered row goes through: a reset that could be dropped from the observer on its own would silently turn the backstop back into "time since the run started", and reclaim a long run that is still delivering.

list.title: latestRows.itemsFromResponse
list.description:
The raw items one latest-media response lets the row show, or invalid when the row must be treated as "failed".

Only an ok response is authoritative. No answer and a not-ok response return invalid — none of them says what the library holds, and an "ok" with an empty list REMOVES the row (HomeRows' populateRowFromData). Not-ok includes a 200 whose body holds no list: the request is a list request (ApiClient.listReq), so the pool reports that body as not-ok and an ok one always carries an roArray (apiResponse.enforceShape). Books are dropped: the app can't present them (issue #525).

list.title: latestRows.removalIsDeferrable
list.description:
May a row's removal be held back until the current latest-rows run ends?

Only for the rows THAT run delivers. A run coalesces one row-size recompute per structural change into one for the whole run, which is only safe while the row list and the three geometry arrays stay in step — so the removals have to wait alongside the recompute.

Every other Home section (Continue Watching, Next Up, On Now, Active Recordings) removes and recomputes immediately, mid-run or not. Two reasons, and the second is load-bearing:

  • Those sections are fired by startParallelLoads, which RACES the orchestrator. Whether one lands inside a run depends on which HTTP response wins, so batching them would make a user-visible row collapse race-dependent — same server, two loads, two behaviours.
  • The queue is keyed by sectionId and holds its entry until the run ends. The orchestrator yields each library exactly once per run (see drainReady), so a queued latest_ row cannot be repopulated before the flush. A parallel section CAN be — onProgramsExpired and Home.refresh() both re-fire those tasks mid-run — and the flush would then delete a row that had just been filled.

list.title: latestRows.runIsStalled
list.description:
Has a run been in flight long enough that its orchestrator thread must be gone?

HomeRows skips a refresh while a run is in flight, which is only safe if the in-flight state can never get stuck: a Task thread that crashes never delivers its last child, so the completion check never fires and the guard would freeze Home's latest rows for the life of that Home instance. This is the backstop, and epic #728 is precisely a history of Task threads dying.

Measured from the last row the run DELIVERED, not from its start. apiPipeline charges its budget only while waiting on the server, so a live run with many rows can legitimately outlast PIPELINE_RUN_MS end to end — every row it hands over is its own proof of life. What a live run cannot do is stay silent much longer than its whole budget, PIPELINE_RUN_MS: a wait never outlasts what is left of it. API_WAIT_MS on top is slack for the silent time that is NOT charged — the task thread starting, building its entries before the first row, and one row's transform and hand-off to this thread. Past the two combined it is not a slow run, it is a dead one.

clock drainReady resets)

list.title: mediaSources
list.description:
Fetching a set of items' MediaSources by id.

Two features ask the same question — "which version ids belong to these items?" — and both reach it from a Task thread holding a list of ids:

episodeQueue.collapseCopies(), choosing one copy per episode on a pre-12 server, where the server lists every file of an episode as its own episode the display-progress correction (versionResume's DISPLAY section), mapping a grouped tile back to whichever of its versions is in progress

It lives here rather than inside either of them because neither owns it. Fields=MediaSources is the expensive field on any item query, so asking for it BY ID — rather than for a whole page — is what keeps the cost tied to the few items that need it.

list.title: mediaSources.IDS_PER_REQUEST
list.description: How many ids one request names. Each costs 35 bytes of URL (32 hex + an encoded comma), so 100 keeps a request near 3.5 KB — well inside common request-line limits.

list.title: mediaSources.byIds
list.description:
byIds: Each item's MediaSources, by item id.

The imperative half — runs on a Task thread, blocking, IDS_PER_REQUEST ids per request. An id the server does not answer for is simply ABSENT from the result; every caller reads that as "no versions known" rather than as an error, so a partial answer degrades instead of failing the screen.

list.title: mediaSources.idChunks
list.description: idChunks: The ids split into runs of at most size, in order — one request each.

list.title: module:AlphaKeyboard.onKeyGridRendered
list.description: Position reset button below the keyboard grid, aligned to right edge

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#AuthenticateByName
list.description: Authenticate user by username and password

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildAuthenticateWithQuickConnectRequest
list.description:
Build a request AA to exchange an APPROVED Quick Connect secret for an auth token, for use with fetchAsync() / fetchRes().

The body's field name changed at 10.8.0 — a FINER boundary than the V1/V2 apiVersion split, so it reads the server version directly rather than m.getApiVersion(): 10.7.x: { "Token": secret } (QuickConnectDto.Token, required) 10.8.0+: { "Secret": secret } (QuickConnectDto.Secret, required) Confirmed against every published spec from 10.7.0 to 10.11.8 — the rename lands at exactly 10.8.0, with no version carrying both names.

DON'T BRANCH ON THE ERROR CODE HERE. The spec declares only 400 ("Missing token") plus 503 from 10.11.0, but a live 10.11.11 answered 404 for a secret it had not seen approved — an undeclared code. So a non-ok response means "this secret cannot be exchanged" and nothing finer; quickConnectExchangeFailure (source/utils/quickConnect.bs) owns the one distinction worth making.

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildCancelSeriesTimerRequest
list.description: Build a request AA to cancel a Live TV series recording timer, for use with SubmitSideEffect().

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildCancelTimerRequest
list.description: Build a request AA to cancel a Live TV recording timer, for use with SubmitSideEffect().

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildConnectQuickConnectRequest
list.description:
Build a request AA to poll whether a Quick Connect secret has been approved, for use with fetchAsync() / fetchRes(). Responds 200 with the same QuickConnectResult shape Initiate returned, its Authenticated flag now true once someone approved the code.

An UNKNOWN or EXPIRED secret answers 404 ("Unknown quick connect secret"), declared by EVERY published spec from 10.7.0 to 10.11.8 and corroborated by a live 10.11.11. That is the only signal separating "not approved yet" from "this code is dead", and it is invisible to a caller that only parses the body — which is why this endpoint has to go through the pool (res.statusCode) rather than a sync JSON helper.

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildCreateSeriesTimerRequest
list.description: Build a request AA to create a Live TV series recording timer, for use with fetchRes() or fetchJson().

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildCreateTimerRequest
list.description: Build a request AA to create a Live TV recording timer, for use with fetchRes() or fetchJson().

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildDeleteItemRequest
list.description: Build a request AA to delete an item, for use with SubmitSideEffect().

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildDeleteSubtitleRequest
list.description:
Build a request AA to delete an EXTERNAL subtitle file from an item, for use with fetchRes().

TAKES THE STREAM, NOT AN INDEX, AND THAT IS THE POINT. The server deletes MediaStream.Path unconditionally, and for an EMBEDDED stream that path is the media container — so aiming this at the wrong stream destroys the user's movie, not a subtitle. This used to accept a bare integer and warn the caller in prose to check IsExternal first. Prose is not a guard: the subtitle panel's list was ALSO external-only at the time, so the safety rested on two separate places staying in agreement, and the moment that list grew to include embedded streams (so it could describe the item honestly) the only thing standing between a mis-wired row and a deleted container was a comment. Requiring the stream means the check happens here, once, and cannot be forgotten by a future caller.

A non-external stream returns INVALID rather than raising: callers already treat an invalid request as "cannot do this" (validatedReq does the same when no server URL is set), so refusing degrades into an inert button instead of a crash.

The one hazard left with the caller: Index must come from a FRESH item fetch. A download inserts a subtitle at index 0 and renumbers every other stream, so a stale index deletes the wrong file — or errors (observed as HTTP 400) if it now points past the end.

Unlike download, delete is SYNCHRONOUS end-to-end — the controller awaits RefreshMetadata, so the next GET /Items/{id} already reflects the new stream list (verified: correct at t+0s).

external subtitle, has no index, or the server URL is not set

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildDownloadRemoteSubtitleRequest
list.description:
Build a request AA to have the SERVER download a remote subtitle onto the item, for use with fetchRes() (not SubmitSideEffect — see below).

The response carries NO success information: the controller wraps the download in try/catch, logs any failure, and returns 204 either way, then queues the metadata refresh ASYNCHRONOUSLY (QueueRefresh). A missing provider, absent credentials, and an exhausted daily quota all yield the same 204 as a success. The ONLY honest completion signal is re-fetching the item and diffing its subtitle MediaStreams — see newSubtitleStreams().

list.title: module:ApiClient.ApiClient#BuildInitiateQuickConnectRequest
list.description:
Build a request AA to start a Quick Connect request, for use with fetchAsync() / fetchRes(). The response carries the Secret we poll with and the Code the user types on their other device.

The HTTP METHOD moved at the same boundary as the apiVersion split: apiVersion 1 (10.7.0 - 10.8.13): GET (no POST route exists) apiVersion 2 (10.9.0+): POST (no GET route exists) Confirmed against every published spec from 10.7.0 to 10.11.8: each version declares exactly one of the two verbs, and the swap is at exactly 10.9.0.

Sending the wrong method to a modern server yields 401 ("Quick connect is not active on this server"), which reads as a feature gate but is actually a route mismatch — so the dispatch is load-bearing, not cosmetic. That collision is also why quickConnectInitiateFailure treats 401 as "disabled": it is the same code either way, and a route mismatch is our bug, not something to tell a user.

a true value returns ONLY results whose IsHashMatch is set, which is frequently an empty list.

list.title: module:ApiQueueTask.emitDispatchWindow
list.description: One line per DISPATCH_WINDOW entries taken off the queue: what the coordinator spent per entry deciding whether to skip it (check), handing it to a slot (send), and delivering answers back (deliver, counted per response, so its window is the same entries seen from the other end). Read by the api-dispatch measurement family in scripts/measurements.js.

list.title: module:ApiQueueTask.processNewChildren
list.description: Read all unprocessed children (ApiResultNodes appended by fetchRes callers), extract their request AAs, add to the internal FIFO queue, and dispatch. Periodically prunes processed children to prevent unbounded accumulation.

list.title: module:ApiQueueTask.resolvePoolSlots
list.description: The pool's width is chosen per device class (apiPool.widthFor, stored as m.global.apiPoolWidth), but its slots are separately named globals (apiPool0, apiPool1, ...) that setGlobalNodes() in source/utils/globals.bs creates one guarded block at a time — no-task-fanout rejects launching fresh Task nodes in a loop. Nothing else ties those blocks to the width, so they are checked against it here, in both directions. A slot the width expects but globals.bs never created (a width raised past the blocks that exist) would dispatch to invalid; one created beyond the width is a thread that runs for the whole session and is never used.

list.title: module:ApiQueueTask.runQueueLoop
list.description:
FIFO request queue coordinator (Architecture C — continuous-server).

Receives ApiResultNode children appended by fetchRes() callers. Each node carries the request AA on its 'request' field. The coordinator reads ALL unprocessed children when woken up, dispatches each to the first free ApiTask pool slot, then routes the completed response back to the ApiResultNode so the orchestrator unblocks.

A queued READ whose caller has stopped waiting is completed as abandoned instead of being sent, so the slot goes to the next request. The decision — including which entries are worth the cross-thread check at all — is apiPoolNextDispatch in apiPool.bs ("Skipping a request nobody is waiting for"); this file is its shell.

Why children instead of a shared field: SceneGraph can coalesce port events when multiple Task threads write to the same field in rapid succession — the coordinator would see fewer events than writes, silently losing requests. Children are immune: even if wakeup events coalesce, the coordinator reads ALL pending children from the node tree, so no request is ever lost regardless of timing.

Startup ordering guarantee:

  1. Each ApiTask pool slot sets isReady=true after registering its request observer.
  2. This coordinator waits for ALL pool slots to be ready before registering its own observers and setting isReady=true.
  3. fetchRes() waits for this coordinator's isReady=true before appending children. Result: pool observers → coordinator ready → fetchRes appends. No startup race.

Thread safety: Only this task thread reads/writes m.queue, m.inFlight, and m.processedIndex — no TOCTOU race. Child appends from other threads go through SceneGraph rendezvous.

list.title: module:ApiQueueTask.tryDispatch
list.description: Dispatch queued requests to free pool slots (FIFO). Only ever called from this coordinator's task thread — no concurrent access.

list.title: module:ApiTask.executeRequest
list.description:
Executes a single HTTP request via the shared executeHttpRequest() helper and shapes the roku-requests result into the pool's response AA (invalid URL → an error AA so the waiting orchestrator still unblocks). Auth/timeout/Content-Type live in the helper.

The body is then held to the shape the request declared (apiResponse.enforceShape): a list request whose body holds no list comes back not-ok with error = "unexpectedShape".

list.title: module:ApiTask.runApiLoop
list.description: Continuous-server event loop (Architecture C). Waits for request field writes, executes HTTP via roku-requests, writes response. Never exits — lives for the lifetime of the app alongside the global pool.

  • "forward"/"rewind" are discrete 10s seeks.
  • "replay" seeks backward by playbackInstantReplaySeconds (same setting as video) — matches the Roku platform spec; users wanting loop control use the "loop" command.
  • "skip" advances to the next track.

See https://github.com/rokudev/dev-doc — docs/DEVELOPER/media-playback/voice-controls/transport-controls.md

list.title: module:AuthManager.canActivate
list.description:
canActivate guard — see AuthManager.xml header. Invoked by the router on the render thread during navigateTo, once per guarded route. A cheap SYNCHRONOUS token check only — no network (launch-time AboutMe re-validation stays in the login flow).

currentRequest is the route object the router is resolving; currentRequest.path is the full requested path (incl. any query string), which is exactly what we stash so the post-login replay can resume the original destination.

Returns: true — token present: allow the navigation. { path: "/login" } — no token: stash the requested path for post-login replay and redirect to /login. The router treats any AA with a non-empty path as a redirect command (Router.brs sgrouter_runGuardChecks) — the same shape sgrouter.createRedirectCommand("/login") produces, without pulling the whole router namespace into this guard node.

list.title: module:BaseGridView.loadFilters
list.description: Render-thread filter load, collapsed from GetFiltersTask (Phase-4 pure-fetch Task collapse; see docs/dev/promises.md). Invoked by the presenter via callFunc so the body runs in component-m context, where fetchAsync + auto-abandon work — the presenter is a class, and the auto-abandon plugin only injects into components with onDestroy (which BaseGridView has). The presenter still owns m.apiFilters + the toast; this just fetches and hands the result back via deliverFilters().

list.title: module:BaseGridView.loadLanguageFilters
list.description:
Second leg of the filter load, on 12.0+ servers only: the audio/subtitle language lists, which live on a DIFFERENT endpoint from the rest.

The two are disjoint and neither is a superset — /Items/Filters carries OfficialRatings and Years, /Items/Filters2 carries the language lists — so a client that wants both has to ask twice. Sequential rather than parallel because a promise callback here cannot capture locals, so the first leg's result has to be parked on m anyway; the extra round trip happens once per library load, off the critical path (the grid's own items load independently).

The language leg is strictly OPTIONAL: any failure delivers the first leg's result unchanged and shows no toast. Losing two filter categories is not worth interrupting someone who was not necessarily going to open the panel, and the categories are offered only when their lists arrive non-empty, so the panel is correct either way.

list.title: module:BaseGridView.loadLibraryFromRoute
list.description: Configure the library view from its route. Both in-app navigation and a deep link / cast supply the rich library node as route.context.item (the resolver passes the node it already validated), so there is no fetch here. A missing context node is therefore an unexpected route shape, not a deferred feature — warn rather than silently render nothing.

list.title: module:BaseGridView.offeredViews
list.description:
The views the presenter is currently listing for this library, [] when there is no presenter yet.

Derived from getOptions() rather than from a second list the presenters would also have to maintain: there is one list, so nothing can disagree with it. "Currently" is load-bearing — a presenter's views depend on the server version and on the parent item (a genre folder offers fewer than its library), so this is asked per load, not cached. The cost is one extra options build per library load, the same work SetUpOptions already does once: a handful of translate() calls on the render thread.

list.title: module:BaseGridView.onGenreSkeletonsReady
list.description:
Draw the Genres view's rows before their artwork exists.

The task knows every genre's name as soon as the genre LIST query returns, which is one request rather than one-per-genre — so the list can be on screen long before the samples land. Each row gets its title and a single skeleton placeholder cell: a RowList does not lay out a childless row at all, and that one cell is also what gives the row its slot height.

genreSkeletons carries ids and titles, NOT nodes. Building the rows here rather than shipping them from the task keeps the payload of that cross-thread write small — the rendezvous is priced by what it carries. Same split of work as HomeRows.createSkeletonRows().

Nothing here is authoritative: content still arrives later with the real rows and replaces these wholesale. If it never arrives, the skeletons are what the failure looks like, which beats an empty screen.

list.title: module:BaseGridView.revealGenreList
list.description:
Swaps the genre RowList to a new set of rows and reveals it, preserving the user's position. ONE owner for both delivery stages — the skeleton rows and the real rows — so the opacity/focus/spinner sequence cannot drift between them.

rowsRoot is a DETACHED ContentNode root: building rows off-tree and assigning content once is a single change notification instead of one per row (the same shape onAlphaSelectedChanged already uses).

Focus/scroll: the view is interactive from the moment skeletons draw, so the user may have scrolled before the real rows land. Skeleton and real rows are 1:1 in server order, so the previous [row, item] position is index-stable — restore it rather than letting the content swap snap the list back to the top. The item index is clamped: a skeleton row holds one cell, the filled row up to 7.

list.title: module:CaptionRenderer.applyFont
list.description:
Applies the downloaded fallback font, or a system font when it is not on disk.

The answer comes from the fetch task (fontAvailable), not from a setting and not from a filesystem probe here: CreateObject("roFileSystem") returns Invalid on the render thread, where this component lives (measured 2026-09-22 — it faulted &hec here while the identical code was fine in the Task this component was split out of).

Asking the SETTING instead would be wrong in the case that matters: playbackSubsCustom being on is what TRIGGERS the download, not proof that it succeeded. A server that cannot supply the font leaves the setting on and the file absent, which is exactly when non-Latin subtitles need the fallback most.
